teaching.causalExplanation: More. Burning joins oxygen atoms to the magnesium atoms, so the oxide carries the magnesium's mass plus the oxygen's. You can see it in the lab. When a strip of magnesium is heated in a crucible, the reading on the balance goes up. That's the opposite of our copper sulfate, which lost mass as water left. Here, something joins instead. But by how much? We can't read grams from the equation, because its coefficients count moles, not grams. So every mass problem crosses a bridge through moles. Step one, write the balanced equation, and read the mole ratio for the two substances in the question. Step two, turn the mass of the given substance into moles, with n equals m over M M. Step three, use the ratio to get moles of the wanted substance. Step four, turn those moles back into a mass, with m equals n times M M. Mass to moles, moles across, moles to mass. Let's do the magnesium. The equation is two M g plus O two makes two M g O, so magnesium and magnesium oxide react two to two, which is one to one. That makes sense, because every magnesium atom ends up in one unit of the oxide. Magnesium's molar mass is about twenty-four point three, so ten point zero grams is zero point four one one moles.
